extracted.intended_audience: theologians, clergy, and learned readers studying Christian doctrine and biblical interpretation
extracted.subtask_short: doctrinal treatise on purgatory and spirits
extracted.subtask_description: A doctrinal/theological exposition arguing against Purgatory and against a natural immortality of the soul, with related discussion of consecration rites and daemonology; aimed at interpreting Scripture and church practice. Contains hermeneutic guidance and examples from biblical texts and ecclesiastical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremonies must be decent and significant
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing rites (e.g., consecrations), the ceremonies, words, and gestures should be both decent and significant, or at least conformable to the action itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Moses anointed the Tabernacle and washed/ anointed Aaron without exorcised water; Solomon blessed, prayed, and offered sacrifice without procession or impertinent words borrowed from other occasions. Avoid introducing ceremonies (e.g., spittle applied to the nose, 'In odorem suavitatis') that lack Scriptural warrant or are impertinent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exorcisms in consecration rites
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural consecrations were performed without exorcisms; rites of consecration do not require driving away phantasms by exorcism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances given: Moses' consecration used anointing oil; Aaron was washed and anointed; Solomon's dedication involved blessing and prayer not exorcism. Therefore, consecrations should not adopt exorcism rituals absent clear warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import irrelevant words or gestures into rites
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonies should not include words or actions 'spoken upon another occasion' or otherwise impertinent to the present action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text condemns using phrases or acts (like application of spittle with a foreign formula) that cannot be justified by authority or reason for that particular rite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural claims of the soul's immortality must be read in context (immortality as grace, not nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The immortality of the soul separated from the body is not proved by Scripture as a natural property of mankind but as given by special grace to the elect; many texts said to prove natural immortality are ambiguous and must be compared with other passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare passages (e.g., Ecclesiastes 12:7, 3:19–21, 4:3, 9:5) and prefer readings consistent with the broader scriptural teaching (see Job 14 discussion). Instances like Enoch's translation show exceptional, grace-dependent cases, not universal natural immortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer harmonious, comparative reading of Scripture over isolated literalism
rubrics_metrics.description: A text should be interpreted with regard to other clear passages; apparent straightforward readings that contradict wider Scripture should be re-examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Solomon's statements about spirit/dust may mean 'God knows' rather than asserting natural immortality. Interpret difficult verses in light of broader canonical teaching (e.g., Job 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'everlasting' language with care (may denote enduring punishment via succession rather than individual eternal torments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'everlasting fire' or 'everlasting punishments' do not necessarily prove that individual wicked persons live eternally in torment; such language can describe continual punishment or the persistence of the punitive state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can read 'everlasting death' as permitting repeated generations of wicked humans to be punished in succession, so the continuance of punishment need not imply the eternal individual life in torment of each damned person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish resurrection to life (elect) from resurrection to punishment (reprobate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture indicates the elect will rise to eternal, spiritual bodies while the reprobate will rise to receive punishment; one should not infer identical eternal life for the reprobate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use texts on resurrection (1 Cor. 15; Luke 20:34–36) to show elect obtain 'incorruptible' bodies and 'die no more'; no Scripture proves reprobate will be glorified like angels or made wholly immortal in the same sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not found doctrines (e.g., Purgatory) on forced or strained readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that require 'hard straining' of texts or rhetorical uses by Fathers to be stretched into literal doctrine are unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: David's fasting for Saul and Jonathan can be explained as honor or personal grief, not evidence of a state where the dead can be aided by the living; many Old Testament phrases (anger, fire, purging) were rhetorically used and later re-applied to support Purgatory without solid basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect ordinary linguistic and metaphorical usage; do not invent unprecedented metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not attribute metaphorical meanings to words (e.g., 'baptism') where that metaphorical use has no precedent in Scripture or ordinary language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text rejects reading 'baptism for the dead' as a metaphor for fasting/prayer/alms since such metaphorical use of 'baptism' has no example; instead consider alternatives like vicarious undertakings or other contextual readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify 'worlds' consistently when interpreting 'world to come'
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretations that equate 'world to come' with a purgatorial intermediate state conflict with a three-world schema (pre-flood, present until judgment, and post-judgment world) and thus are inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'world to come' (post-judgment) is agreed to have no purgatory; therefore Matthew 12:32 should not be read as promising post-mortem purification in a 'world to come.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider historical and ecclesial context when reading sayings about forgiveness (e.g., Matthew 12:32)
rubrics_metrics.description: When Jesus says words will or will not be forgiven 'in this world, nor in the world to come,' consider whether he is forecasting pastoral practice or Church severity rather than teaching a doctrine of post-mortem purgation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One suggested reading: the saying contrasts Jesus' readiness to forgive with future pastors' intransigence (i.e., ecclesiastical discipline), which could explain its wording without invoking purgatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret images of refining fire as eschatological purification at judgment, not intra-mortem purgatorial burning
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages about passing through fire or being refined (e.g., 1 Cor. 3, Zach. 13) refer to the refining at the day of judgment and renewal of the world, not to a post-mortem purgatorial fire for incorporeal souls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'fire' in such passages as the eschatological trial that tests and refines works at the final appearing of Christ; do not convert these images into support for the burning of disembodied souls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not literalize parables or allegories to establish doctrinal technicalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Parables (e.g., Dives and Lazarus) are not reliable literal evidence for technical doctrines like the state of the dead; they may serve moral or illustrative purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read parables as instructional stories rather than detailed metaphysical expositions of the afterlife; avoid building dogma on singular parabolic details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish usefulness of prayers for the dead from proof of Purgatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if prayers for the dead are not useless (e.g., if God could convert some after death before resurrection), their usefulness does not establish the institutional reality of Purgatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author allows that prayers for the dead may have some pastoral or hopeful value but insists this does not prove a middle state into which souls are placed and purified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read 'baptism for the dead' in light of plausible social/practical explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than positing a doctrine of post-mortem change, consider cultural practices (e.g., acting as sureties for deceased persons) or other plausible interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One reading: early Christians sometimes stood surety for absent persons or undertook responsibilities for those not yet able to profess faith; such practices could explain the phrase without implying Purgatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret threatening legal metaphors (e.g., Matthew 5:25) as relating to present life and judgment, not evidence of post-mortem purgation
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegories about prison, officers, and paying the uttermost farthing describe urgency in this life and consequences at judgment; they do not establish a distinct purgatorial state after death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the allegory's intended moral/legal force (repent now, settle with adversary) rather than seeing it as a technical description of post-mortem processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not construct a multi-tiered post-mortem judicial system from isolated sayings
rubrics_metrics.description: Matthew 5's tripartite mention of sins and punishments (râcha, fool, hellfire) was rhetorical about inward lawfulness, not an account of multiple courts/punitive tribunals after death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the passage with its immediate explanatory context (Jesus' reinterpretation of the Mosaic law) rather than as evidence for differentiated post-mortem punishments or purgatorial grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain apparitions and phantasms by natural physiological/psychological causes when plausible
rubrics_metrics.description: Visions, apparitions, and phantasms commonly arise from impressions on the organs of sight or other bodily causes (e.g., pressure on the eye, continuing motion after stimulus) and need not be attributed to incorporeal external entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pressure on the eye producing light; dreams and imagination continuing after the external cause is removed. Prefer natural explanations before hypothesizing airy or aethereal beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming ancient 'daemons' were incorporeal independent beings without examining cognitive/perceptual accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient peoples often interpreted internal images as external beings (daemons); this misattribution explains the origin of daemonologies and cult practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat daemonology as a social/institutional response to perceived apparitions (used by rulers and poets to regulate society), not proof of immaterial spirits inhabiting air or other subtile matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Scripture speaks of spirits 'entering' someone, consider moral-intentional readings rather than literal invasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'Satan entered into Judas' can be read as describing Judas's hostile or traitorous intention rather than a literal demonic possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogously, 'Holy Ghost' in certain contexts denotes graces and good inclinations; interpret 'entering' language as describing internal dispositions or intentions when that reading fits the context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat miraculous or supernatural-sounding motions (led by the Spirit, carried by the devil) as visions or figurative language when literal sense is impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of being 'led in the Spirit' or 'carried by the devil' can be visions or figurative expressions; do not insist on literal physical carrying or possession when context indicates visionary/figurative meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare parallel Gospel accounts (e.g., differing verbs in Matthew vs Luke) and prefer the interpretation that fits natural possibility and literary genre (vision, prophetic transport).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer incorporeal, immaterial spirits as taught by Scripture without clear textual warrant
rubrics_metrics.description: The author finds no clear Scriptural place proving incorporeal spirits distinct from bodily forms; terms like 'spirit' often denote the Holy Ghost, dispositions, or bodily (non-flesh/bone) realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read 'spirit' with caution; where Scripture links 'spirit' and bodily action (e.g., 'spirit' led Jesus), consider that the Bible may conceive spiritual activity in bodily or quasi-bodily terms rather than as purely immaterial entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand exorcistic language as signifying God's word-power over maladies and disorderly states
rubrics_metrics.description: When Christ commands a 'devil' to go out, this may signify the divine power to cure madness, fever, or other disorders, and the speech-act demonstrates God’s authority rather than addressing an actual incorporeal agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogize to commanding wind or sea; such commands illustrate the power of God's word. Thus cures and expulsions should be read as demonstrations of divine authority over illness and disorder rather than proof of immaterial possessors.
